Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestion to discuss how natural sunlight could be managed to realize our photothermal concept in practical devices. We envision two possible approaches for implementing the proposed photothermal perovskite-based electrochemical system in a commercialization context. The first is to employ NIR sheet irradiation to induce photothermal effects across a large-area catalyst. However, achieving a significant photothermal contribution in this manner would require the use of NIR lasers with relatively high intensity, which may lead to considerable energy loss and thus limit the practicality of this approach. Therefore, to practically implement this technology, it is essential to develop a sheet- type irradiation system with minimized NIR power loss.
The second approach, as suggested by the reviewer, is to utilize natural sunlight irradiation to induce the photothermal effect. One possible strategy is to spectrally split natural sunlight so that the NIR component is directed toward the catalyst while the remaining visible range is absorbed by the perovskite layer. In fact, previous studies have already demonstrated the use of spectral-split optics to simultaneously drive BiVO and perovskite photoelectrodes 4 (Adv. Funct. Mater. 2022, 32, 2110284). Therefore, by adopting a similar architecture, it should be feasible to selectively extract NIR from solar light and deliver it to the catalyst to induce a pronounced photothermal effect. However, the temperature rise achievable under direct sunlight alone is insufficient to generate a meaningful photothermal response. To overcome this limitation, a Fresnel lens can be employed. Fresnel lenses have already been applied to Si solar panels, where they concentrate sunlight onto the absorber layer. By combining spectral- splitting and Fresnel lens concentration, a sufficient NIR flux could be harvested to induce the desired photothermal effect on catalyst, thereby enabling a photothermal perovskite-based electrochemical system driven solely by natural sunlight. We have incorporated this discussion into our revised manuscript to highlight the practical applicability of this concept. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion, which allowed us to refine and expand the discussion with greater technical depth.

Regarding EIS, the key question is what resistance the low-frequency (LF) arc
represents. Because our device uses a perovskite/spiro/Au stack, a positive LF arc attributable to recombination/ion migration in the bulk or at perovskite interfaces can indeed appear, as the reviewer notes. To disentangle contributions observed at the cathode, we fabricated two devices separating the components: (i) an encapsulated photovoltaic (PV) stack electrically contacted with a Cu wire at the catalyst position but without the catalyst itself, and (ii) a catalyst electrode (FTO/CC/Pt-C). For the encapsulated PV stack, the LF arc emerges and increases as the bias moves from open circuit toward short-circuit (Fig. R3b). Bode analysis shows this resistance appears around ~1–10 Hz and its characteristic frequency shifts to lower values as the bias approaches short-circuit (Fig. R3c). These features are consistent with the Shockley–Read–Hall (SRH) recombination resistance originating from the bulk and/or interfaces, as reported in prior literature (Adv. Energy Mater. 2024, 14, 2400955). For the isolated catalyst electrode, an LF arc is also observed; however, its magnitude decreases as the potential is swept negative from the onset voltage, and it is further reduced under NIR illumination (Fig. R3d, e). We attribute this behavior to charge-transfer resistance at the catalyst/electrolyte interface: both improved kinetics and mass transport under NIR illumination decrease this resistance. In the Bode plots, this LF contribution appears near ~1–10 Hz and shifts to higher characteristic frequencies as the potential approaches onset and the peak frequency increases further to ~10– 50 Hz with NIR illumination (Fig. R3f). These control experiments demonstrate that (i) SRH- related and charge-transfer resistances can occupy similar frequency windows, and (ii) the LF- arc trend at the working cathode mirrors the charge-transfer behavior of the catalyst electrode but is opposite to the SRH recombination-related trend of the encapsulated PV. Consequently, interpreting the cathode LF arc as charge-transfer resistance is more consistent with the observed bias and illumination dependences. However, we need to explain why the SRH- related LF resistance observed in the encapsulated PV structure does not appear at the cathode.
This interpretation aligns with prior PEC-EIS analyses (Adv. Energy Mater. 2021, 11, 2003569), which recommend bias-dependent assignments of the LF arc. Near the onset voltage, charge transfer is typically the dominant bottleneck and thus the most likely origin of the LF arc. ## Abstract

Perovskite-based solar water splitting systems are promising candidates for addressing environmental challenges, exceeding the commercialization efficiency of solar-to-hydrogen (STH) at >10%. However, the operational stability remains suboptimal due to insufficient in situ/operando insights into charge carrier dynamics. Here, we investigate the role of charge accumulation on operational stability through operando catalytic modulation via near-infrared (NIR) toggling on a photothermal catalyst. Electrochemical analyses under operando NIR toggling demonstrate enhanced hydrogen evolution reaction kinetics and reduced charge recombination. In situ analyses confirm that reduced charge accumulation suppresses ion migration in the perovskite layer, thereby enhancing operational stability. The NIR-irradiated cathode delivers a photocurrent density of 25.48 mA cm–2, maintaining 90% of its initial photocurrent density at 0 V RHE for 310 h. A parallelly-illuminated coplanar system with NIR-irradiated perovskite-based water splitting cathode operates without bias, achieving a STH efficiency of 15.18%, retaining 70% of their initial performance for 115 h.

---

## Introduction

Solar water splitting systems have been extensively studied as a promising solution to the escalating energy crisis and environmental degradation caused by fossil fuel dependency1,2. Recently, devices utilizing lead halide perovskite photo-absorbers have been at the forefront of research due to their exceptional optoelectronic properties, including low exciton binding energy, high charge transport efficiency, long carrier diffusion length, and tunable band gaps3–8. Despite their low moisture tolerance, various conductive encapsulation strategies have been developed to prevent water permeation and suppress performance loss9–16. Due to the optimal features of perovskites and advancements in encapsulation approaches, immersed perovskite-based water splitting systems have achieved an unbiased solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency of 13.4% in aqueous environments, surpassing the commercial efficiency threshold of 10%17,18. However, even with complete prevention of water permeation through fully encapsulated structures, the operational stability of perovskite water splitting systems remains significantly suboptimal and is much lower compared to their photovoltaic (PV) counterparts9,19–21.

Prolonged exposure to factors such as heat, UV light, and electric fields is known to deteriorate the operational stability of perovskite devices22,23. In addition, a notable difference between perovskite water splitting systems and PV cells arises with the integration of an electrochemical compartment into the device. This introduces a timescale mismatch between photocarrier generation at the picosecond scale and electrochemical reactions at the microsecond scale24,25. This substantial discrepancy in timescales can induce charge accumulation within the multilayer device, compromising stability during continuous illumination26,27. Previous studies have focused on interface engineering of the carrier transport layer and the incorporation of efficient catalysts to mitigate these issues in perovskite-based water splitting systems9,15–17,19,21,28–36. Despite these efforts, it remains challenging to directly monitor charge accumulation dynamics within perovskite layers due to the lack of operando evaluations on the same device under operational conditions. Also, they have predominantly been limited to ex situ assessments, thereby hindering a comprehensive understanding of charge accumulation impacts during actual device operation.

Temperature modulation of electrochemical reactions offers a viable approach for mitigating and monitoring charge accumulation under operando conditions, provided it does not damage the temperature-sensitive internal layers of the device37–41. This strategy can also enhance the performance and kinetics of the state-of-the-art electrochemical catalysts. However, conventional heating methods require substantial energy because of the high heat capacity of water and pose a risk of degrading the photo-absorber along with surrounding layers. The photothermal effect, which induces localized temperature elevation in targeted areas upon simple irradiation with near-infrared (NIR) light, presents an ideal solution to this challenge42. To fully exploit the benefits of localized temperature modulation through the photothermal effect without causing thermal conduction to the perovskite layer, a recently developed catalyst-decoupled structure with thermally insulating epoxy resin can be employed14,15 (Supplementary Fig. 1). This lateral architecture allows independent thermal manipulation of the catalyst, in contrast to traditional vertical configurations where encapsulating materials with high thermal conductivity could adversely affect the perovskite layers. By integrating photothermal effects and advanced catalysts into the above-mentioned lateral design, electrochemical reaction kinetics can be modulated through toggling of NIR irradiation, enabling direct operando observation of carrier dynamics within the perovskite layer of the same device (Supplementary Note 1).

Inspired by such applicability of the photothermal effect, we investigate the electrochemical behavior of an immersed perovskite-based water splitting electrode paired with a commercial Pt-carbon-coated carbon cloth (Pt-C/CC) catalyst. NIR laser irradiation of the catalyst elevates its temperature via the photothermal effect, thereby improving the overall performance of the device, in operando. Electrochemical analyses under operando manipulation demonstrate not only enhanced hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) kinetics but also reduced charge accumulation within the multilayer structure. In a hybrid device combining a water splitting cell and a solar cell, in situ monitoring during operational stability tests reveal that reduced charge accumulation suppresses ion migration within the perovskite layer via accelerated electrochemical kinetics, thus improving long-term stability. Our results identify catalyst degradation as the dominant factor in the initial stages of stability decay, while perovskite degradation become more significant in later stages, thereby elucidating the degradation mechanism of the immersed perovskite-based solar water splitting system. Through this understanding, we demonstrate that charge accumulation is a primary cause of performance deterioration, significantly impacting overall stability. The NIR-irradiated perovskite cathode delivers a photocurrent density of 25.48 mA cm–2, retaining over 90% of its initial photocurrent density (t90) under continuous 1-sun illumination at 0 V RHE for 310 h. Coupling a perovskite-based water splitting anode with the improved cathode, a parallelly illuminated coplanar system operates without applied bias, achieving a STH efficiency of 15.18% while maintaining 70% of its initial performance (t70) for 115 h.

## Results

Design and performance of immersed perovskite-based water splitting cathode

The device configuration and performance of perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are detailed in Supplementary Note 2. Based on the PSCs, a perovskite-based water splitting cathode was fabricated by positioning a Cu tape and Cu wire on the top Au electrode (Fig. 1a) (see Supplementary Fig. 2, Supplementary Note 3 and 4, and Methods for additional fabrication details about the device). The Pt-C/CC photothermal catalyst was placed at the bottom electrode, physically separated from the perovskite. All experiments were conducted under ambient conditions (RH 15–20%, 23–25 °C), unless specified. The temperature elevation of the catalyst on the cathode, immersed in 0.5 M KPi (potassium phosphate) (pH 7) electrolyte under NIR irradiation, was monitored via thermal imaging using an infrared camera, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. The catalyst’s temperature increased significantly within a short period despite being submerged in the electrolyte, while epoxy encapsulation effectively prevented heat transfer to the photo-absorber layer. The HER performance of the cathode was evaluated using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) (Fig. 1b) (see Supplementary Fig. 4 for the detailed experimental setup of performance measurements with NIR irradiation). Despite being immersed in the electrolyte, the perovskite-based cathode stably operated without any degradation, indicating that our encapsulation strategy effectively prevented water permeation (Supplementary Fig. 5). The NIR laser intensity used was 2.5 A, with the optimization process described in Supplementary Fig. 6. The immersed perovskite-based cathode initially demonstrated a saturated photocurrent density (Jph) of 24.08 mA cm–2 at 0 V RHE (V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode) and an onset voltage (Von) of 0.96 V RHE. Notably, following NIR laser irradiation of the catalyst, the cathode’s performance improved, exhibiting a Jph of 25.48 mA cm–2 at 0 V RHE and Von of 1.04 V RHE. The increased onset voltage under NIR irradiation originates from enhanced catalyst performance (detailed explanation in later sections, see Supplementary Fig. 22), rather than change in band gap or photovoltage provided by the perovskite layer. Note that the thermodynamic potential of the HER does not vary due to the catalyst surface temperature (Supplementary Note 5). Operando performance observations were conducted with the NIR laser alternately turned on and off (Supplementary Fig. 7). The dark current of the water splitting cell was measured respective to the NIR irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 8). The presented dark current data via various measurements that the photocurrent density under light illumination originates from photo-induced processes rather than unfavorable attributions such as current leakages or side reactions apart from HER. Enhanced performance was observed under NIR irradiation, which reverted to the original control (without NIR) levels when the NIR laser was turned off. This indicates that the increased temperature enhanced the catalytic activity of Pt-C/CC, leading to improved overall performance of the cathode.

The incident photon-to-current conversion efficiency (IPCE) spectra demonstrated enhanced photon harvesting across all wavelengths, with integrated IPCE values under NIR irradiation closely matching the measured Jph values from LSV curves (Fig. 1c). The improvement in IPCE across the entire wavelength range suggests that the photothermal effect induced by NIR irradiation increased the catalyst’s temperature, thereby accelerating HER kinetics and enhancing both Jph and Von. Additionally, the unchanged absorption wavelength range of the IPCE spectra under both control and NIR-irradiated conditions indicates that the temperature increase of catalyst due to NIR irradiation is local and does not alter the band gap of the perovskite layer due to the thermal insulation of epoxy resin. By comparing the in situ photoluminescence (PL) spectra before and after NIR irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 9), it was observed that the PL peak position remained unchanged, and the intensity also maintained the same, which is consistent with IPCE results.

The contribution of NIR irradiation to the power of immersed perovskite-based cathode was quantitatively evaluated by measuring the improvement in the fill factor (FF) (Supplementary Fig. 10). The maximum power point (MPP) shifted to a more anodic potential (from 0.77 to 0.86 V RHE), indicating that NIR irradiation on the catalyst significantly elevated both photocurrent and photovoltage. The FF was calculated using the equation:

FF(%) = (JMPP × VMPP) / (Jph × Von) × 100% (1)

where JMPP and VMPP are the current density and potential at the MPP, respectively. The FF of control device increased from 70.07% to 77.41% upon NIR laser irradiation. This improvement in FF indicates that the photothermal effect enhances catalytic activity, leading to reduced power losses in the saturation region and increased HER reactivity even at lower voltage inputs. Notably, the cathode under NIR irradiation achieved an applied bias photon-to-current conversion efficiency (ABPE) of 20.69%. Performance parameters of 16 different devices are summarized in Supplementary Figs. 11–13 and Supplementary Table 1, demonstrating consistent performance enhancement with NIR irradiation.

The long-term stability of the cathode was evaluated chronoamperometrically under continuous 1-sun illumination at 0 V RHE (Fig. 1d). Stability tests were conducted without additional stirring systems to better assess the effects of the photothermal catalyst. The Jph of the control device declined rapidly, falling below 90% of its initial value within just 6 h of operation. In contrast, the NIR-irradiated device demonstrated a stable performance over 310 h, maintaining 90% of its initial Jph. The photocurrent drop observed in the final stage of the stability measurement for the NIR sample resulted from intentionally switching the light source off and on to confirm that the device was still responsive to illumination. For the control device, a rapid current decrease was observed during the initial stage of stability measurement, with a degradation rate of 0.52 mA cm–2 h–1 at 8 h, leading to a reduction to ~80% of the initial Jph. In comparison, the NIR-irradiated device exhibited a lower degradation rate of 0.04 mA cm–2 h–1 at 8 h, consistently preserving the initial Jph over an extended period. It is notable to mention that the effect of Pt dissolution from the counter electrode and redeposition on working electrode is neglectable, since the system operates in a potentiostatic condition within a neutral pH medium (Supplementary Fig. 14). Also, the electrolyte temperature has remained nearly constant throughout the experiment, indicating that the enhancement in stability was not influenced by temperature (Supplementary Fig. 15). Additionally, the control device exhibited a longer average Jph fluctuation period of 180.13 s, whereas the NIR-irradiated device showed a shorter average period of 30.6 s (Supplementary Fig. 16). The initial decay of Jph and current fluctuations are closely related to catalyst stability, influenced by bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, and departure), which is discussed in later sections. The operational stability statistics of the control and NIR-irradiated cathodes are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 17, highlighting the enhanced stability of the cathode under NIR irradiation and suggesting a correlation between improved electrochemical reaction kinetics and overall device stability. To evaluate the effect of stirring on cathode stability, performance and stability tests were conducted with and without stirring. When stirring was applied, the overpotential decreased compared to the unstirred condition, which can be attributed to improved mass transport near the catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 18a). The stability test also revealed slightly enhanced durability under stirring, indicating that increased mass transport at the catalyst–electrolyte interface contributes to improved device stability (Supplementary Fig. 18b). Notably, however, the stability achieved by stirring alone did not reach the level observed under NIR irradiation. This suggests that NIR illumination not only promotes mass transport and bubble departure but also enhances the HER kinetics, thereby suppressing charge accumulation. Such kinetic acceleration under NIR irradiation appears to play a significant role in further improving long-term stability. Furthermore, stability test under 0.5-sun illumination was conducted (Supplementary Fig. 19). The device exhibited enhanced stability compared to the original control sample, maintaining ~90% of the initial photocurrent for about 56 h. This improvement can be attributed to the reduced number of photogenerated carriers under the low-sun illumination, which reduces charge accumulation and consequently enhances the overall device stability. These results further highlight the critical role of kinetics of electrochemical reaction in determining stability of the perovskite-based water splitting device. Moreover, an encapsulated PV structure was fabricated in which the catalyst attached to the FTO side of the cathode was replaced with a Cu wire. The resulting device exhibited an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.1 V and a short-circuit current density (Jsc) of about 25.1 mA cm–2 (Supplementary Fig. 20a). The device stability under both 1.05 V (near OCV) and 0 V (short-circuit, SC) conditions (Supplementary Fig. 20b). Notably, these stability tests were carried out while the device was immersed in electrolyte, closely replicating the cathode operating environment. Under near OCV conditions the device showed limited stability, with a t90 (time to reach 90% of the initial photocurrent) of 3 h. In contrast, under SC conditions the photocurrent retained nearly 90% of its initial value for more than 25 h. Considering that the control cathode exhibits a t90 of about 6 h, the stability trend can be summarized as encapsulated PV (near OCV) < cathode (control) < encapsulated PV (SC). These results indicate that charge consumption significantly influences the intrinsic stability of the perovskite layer. The H2 gas production rate of the NIR-irradiated device was measured over time using gas chromatography (GC) analysis (Fig. 1e), with the Faradaic efficiency of H2 evolution determined to be 98.29%. A comparative analysis of performance and stability values of previously reported immersed perovskite-based electrodes is summarized in Supplementary Fig. 21 and Supplementary Table 2.

Photothermal effect inducing HER kinetic improvement on electrocatalyst (EC)

To validate the enhancement of HER catalytic activity via the photothermal effect on the catalyst, the electrocatalytic properties of Pt-C/CC/FTO electrodes were evaluated in 0.5 M KPi (Supplementary Fig. 22a, 51a). The LSV curves indicated that the potentials required to achieve a current density of 10 mA cm–2 were –0.15 V RHE for the control and –0.11 V RHE under NIR irradiation. The Tafel slopes were determined to be 40.8 mV dec–1 for the control and 27.6 mV dec–1 under NIR irradiation, demonstrating accelerated catalytic activity under NIR irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 22b). Note that the Tafel slope is strongly dependent not only on temperature but also on the coverage of reaction intermediates and the rate-determining step43,44. Under NIR irradiation, the local heating and improved charge-transfer kinetics likely suppressed the excessive hydrogen coverage on Pt, leading to a more favorable surface condition for the Heyrovsky step. Furthermore, the enhancement could have resulted from the increased mass transport due to a forced convection via local heating. These effects are described in detail in later sections; however, it is necessary to confirm that electrochemical kinetics enhance under NIR irradiation, since HER overpotential originates from both mass transport and kinetic limitations. Control experiments of Pt-C/CC/FTO performance under (i) strong stirring condition (Video S1) and (ii) a thin electrolyte environment was conducted (Supplementary Fig. 23a–c). As shown in the video, vigorous stirring was imposed to establish a condition in which mass transport around the catalyst is strongly enhanced, and then compared the performance of the Pt-C/CC/FTO electrode with and without NIR irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 23d). Under stirring, the performance increased, and it improved further upon NIR irradiation. These results originate from the enhancement of further mass transport but also reaction kinetics since the limitation in mass transport has been alleviated to an extent before the NIR irradiation. In the second control experiment, the catalyst was immersed to a minimal depth such that only an ultra thin electrolyte layer was formed at the surface (Supplementary Fig. 23e). This configuration suppresses mass transport at the catalyst surface, but more importantly it prevents the formation of a sufficient temperature gradient to drive forced convection under NIR irradiation, thus separating mass transport and convection from reaction kinetics under NIR. Even under these conditions, NIR irradiation still increased the performance, which we attribute to an intrinsic kinetic enhancement. This results in a lower apparent Tafel slope despite the elevated temperature. To further elucidate the factors contributing to the increased catalytic activity, the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was measured by calculating the electrochemical double-layer capacitance (Cdl) (Supplementary Fig. 24). The ECSA values were 34.5 cm2 for the control and 42.9 cm2 under NIR irradiation, confirming an increase in the active area due to thermal activation (Supplementary Table 3). Also, to confirm that the increase in ECSA did not originate from an irreversible morphological change of the electrode due to NIR irradiation, the ECSA variation of electrode was observed after being cooled for 3 min and 10 min, respectively. After 3 min of cooling, ECSA was reduced to 37.5 cm2 and further decreased after 10 min, approaching the pre-irradiation value of 34.5 cm2. Based on the LSV curves of the catalyst electrode, the local heating was evaluated (Supplementary Note 6). The increased ECSA under thermal activation is likely attributed to changes in the quantity of adsorbates on the catalyst during operation. To investigate this effect, in situ Raman spectroscopy was performed on the Pt-C/CC/FTO electrode under conditions identical to the LSV measurements to monitor adsorbate changes during operation45 (Fig. 2a; detailed electrode sampling and experimental setup are shown in Supplementary Fig. 25a–c). Without an applied bias, the characteristic D- and G-band peaks of carbon cloth and carbon powder from Pt-C were observed at 1340 cm–1 and 1580 cm–1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 25d). Upon increasing the applied bias to –0.2 V RHE, the peaks exhibited minimal shifts, suggesting insufficient chemical bonding with adsorbates to cause observable changes. When the applied bias was increased to –0.3 V RHE, a decrease in peak intensities was noted, indicating interactions with adsorbates in the electrolyte. A significant reduction in the original peaks was observed only when the bias reached –0.4 V RHE, as the electrode began interacting with a substantial quantity of adsorbates, likely including water molecules and alkali metal ions45,46 (i.e., potassium ions from KPi). Concurrent with the depletion of the D- and G-band peaks, a new peak emerged around 1642 cm–1, corresponding to interactions between water molecules and Pt particles, consistent with literature45. Under NIR irradiation, the same electrode showed similar peak dissipation and the emergence of the Pt-H2O interaction at a reduced bias of –0.2 V RHE, demonstrating decreased overpotential required to induce similar adsorbate interactions, further supporting the photothermal effect’s role in enhancing catalytic activity. Furthermore, the catalytic activity of Pt-C/CC was normalized to the respective ECSA values to compare electrochemical kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 26). The specific current density per ECSA (Js) was calculated using the equation:

Js = Jg × A / ECSA (2)

where A is the geometric area of the electrode, and Jg is the current density per geometric area. The NIR-irradiated catalyst exhibited a distinctly steeper Js slope compared to the control, even after ECSA normalization, indicating enhanced electrochemical kinetics. These combined results elucidate the effects of thermal activation on the catalyst in two aspects: increased electrochemical active area density and improved HER kinetics.

Operando electrochemical analyses of perovskite-based cathode

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed on the immersed perovskite-based cathode under both control and NIR irradiation conditions to assess the impact of thermal activation on catalyst performance. Measurements were conducted at potentials ranging from 1.0 to 0.8 V RHE over a frequency range of 0.1 Hz to 300 kHz under 1-sun illumination. Below 0.8 V RHE, both conditions reached saturation in photocurrent density, hindering accurate measurement of charge transfer resistance. Therefore, EIS measurements were limited to the potential range of 1.0 to 0.8 V RHE. The Nyquist plots (Fig. 2b, c) were fitted using a Voigt-type equivalent circuit model (Supplementary Fig. 27 and Supplementary Note 7), with the fitting calculations summarized in Supplementary Table 4. Regardless of applied potential and NIR irradiation, there were no significant differences in Rs and RHF. However, the Bode plot revealed noticeable differences around the low-frequency region (100–0.1 Hz)47,48 (Supplementary Fig. 28). The low-frequency arc and Rct were significantly reduced under NIR irradiation compared to the control, indicating that the photothermal effect enhances the charge transfer reaction (Fig. 2b, c). A detailed interpretation of the low-frequency arc is provided in Supplementary Note 8. Transient photocurrent analysis (TPC) was performed to observe charge accumulation during operation under both conditions (Supplementary Fig. 29a). Under control conditions, a reverse current, indicative of reverse charge flow due to charge accumulation within the perovskite-based cathode, appeared after the initial decay. The observed reverse current originates from the discharge of trapped charges when the light is turned off. During illumination, some photogenerated carriers are trapped at the perovskite/charge transport layer (CTL) interface. Upon light termination, these trapped charges are released and flow in the opposite direction relative to the photocurrent, which manifests as the reverse current in the TPC signal9,49,50. For the control sample, severe charge accumulation at the catalyst/electrolyte interface interfered the charge separation and transport inside the device, leading to increased charge trapping at the perovskite/CTL interface. As a result, a pronounced reverse current was observed when the light was turned off. In contrast, for the NIR-sample, the improved catalyst kinetics reduced charge accumulation at the catalyst/electrolyte interface, which in turn mitigated charge trapping at the perovskite/CTL boundary. Moreover, intensity-modulated photovoltage spectroscopy (IMVS) was conducted under open circuit conditions with white light illumination bias, using a perturbation of 10% of the light intensity and a frequency range from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz (Supplementary Fig. 29b, c). At ~100 kHz both conditions show high-frequency responses, indicative of fast photocarrier generation. It can be seen in both conditions that these charges are not completely consumed, where it is more severe for the control condition in that the induced photovoltage remains higher than that of the NIR condition throughout the frequency sweep. This can originate from the temporary trapping of these charges rather than forming chemical adsorbates on the electrode surface26,51, which is plausible considering the in situ Raman analysis (Fig. 2a). Although the steady-state net photocurrent is zero at open circuit, the sinusoidal light perturbation gives rise to transient interfacial charge transfer at low frequencies51. Thus, this transient interfacial electron transfer at low frequencies effectively impacts the measured photovoltage. As the intensity modulated illumination reaches low frequency near ~1 Hz, sufficiently slow for the device to undergo charge transfer, a decrease in photovoltage is observed for NIR condition as opposed to further increase in photovoltage in control condition. This is consistent with slow charge transfer at open circuit observed via EIS and thus stronger charge accumulation under control compared to when NIR is applied26,52.

To verify the impact of reduced charge accumulation on charge transport behavior in the cathode, intensity-modulated photocurrent spectroscopy (IMPS) was conducted to assess the rate of interface charge recombination and charge-transfer kinetics in the presence of the photothermal effect29,42. In Fig. 2d, e, the Nyquist plots of the complex photocurrents under control and NIR conditions were obtained under light modulation within the same potential range as EIS measurements. The charge transfer efficiency is determined by the ratio of the real photocurrents at the high- and low-frequency intercepts using the equation:

ktrans = (ktrans + krec) (3)

where ktrans and krec represent the interface recombination and charge-transfer rate constants, respectively53. Normalizing the real photocurrent to the high-frequency intercept allows the low-frequency intercept to directly reflect the charge transfer efficiency. The combined rate, ktrans + krec, is given by 2πfmin, where fmin is the frequency at the apex of the semicircle in the IMPS plots. By combining the charge-transfer efficiency and fmin, both ktrans and krec were obtained (Fig. 2f). The fmin are provided in Supplementary Table 5. As the cathodic potential increased, ktrans rose for both conditions, with the NIR-irradiated condition showing a higher ktrans, indicating that the photothermal effect accelerates HER kinetics, consistent with EIS results. Conversely, krec decreased for both control and NIR conditions with increasing cathodic bias, with krec and its intersection potential with ktrans being lower in the NIR condition than in the control. This indicates that the faster HER kinetics under NIR irradiation reduce interface recombination and facilitate carrier extraction within the cathode, enhancing performance. Moreover, the faster kinetics of the electrochemical reaction reduce charge accumulation and recombination within the perovskite cathode, contributing to improved long-term stability.

Monitoring charge accumulation during long-term operation

Stability measurements in control condition showed that the photocurrent density of the device declined rapidly, followed by a slower reduction rate, eventually reaching a stable level. To investigate the changes in bulk characteristics during each representative stage, we fabricated a device with a structure serving as a hybrid of both a solar water splitting cathode and an encapsulated solar cell (see Supplementary Note 9 and Supplementary Fig. 30). This configuration allowed us to monitor changes in carrier dynamics and band bending within the bulk perovskite using a two-electrode setup, avoiding interference from the electrolyte, catalyst degradation, or electrochemical reactions54. Figure 3a, b present the performance of cathodes under each respective conditions at 0 h, 8 h, and 45 h of operation, characterized by LSV under 1-sun illumination in 0.5 M KPi electrolyte. Performance parameters are summarized in Supplementary Fig. 31 and Supplementary Table 6. Specific time points were selected to represent the two distinct stages observed in the operational stability curve: the initial rapid decline at 8 h and the subsequent stabilization at 45 h. The corresponding long-term stability of the hybrid cathode is shown in Supplementary Fig. 32. After 8 h of operation, both the control and NIR-irradiated samples exhibited only slight decreases in Von and FF, largely retaining their initial performance. As the operation extended to 45 h, the control device showed severe degradation across all performance parameters, retaining only ~53% of its initial photocurrent. In contrast, the NIR-irradiated device maintained a stable LSV profile and demonstrated high stability, preserving ~87% of its initial photocurrent value. Additionally, the enhanced HER kinetics facilitated by the photothermal effect reduced charge accumulation during operation, resulting in a smaller decrease in onset potential after 45 h compared to the control device, aligning well with the LSV results.

We employed drive-level capacitance profiling (DLCP) and capacitance-voltage (C-V) methods to evaluate the carrier density of control and NIR-irradiated samples at 0 h (fresh) and after 8 h and 45 h of operation55,56 (Supplementary Fig. 33 and Supplementary Note 10). The corresponding interfacial trap densities were profiled at various depths for both control and NIR-irradiated devices, as shown in Fig. 3c, d. Both devices exhibited nearly identical trap site densities between the fresh state and 8 h of operation, indicating that the initial stage of operation has a negligible effect on the degradation of the perovskite layer in both control and NIR-irradiated devices. However, beyond 8 h of operation, trap densities increased more significantly on the hole transport layer (HTL) side (spiro-OMeTAD) compared to the SnO2 layer, with this increase being more pronounced in the control device than in the NIR-irradiated device. This result confirms that enhanced charge transfer reactions suppress charge accumulation at the interface of multilayer devices, leading to fewer trap states under NIR irradiation. We infer that the increased trap densities observed in the HTL side during operation are attributed to iodine migration and the organic nature of the HTL layer, which is more susceptible to hole accumulation. Furthermore, KPFM was performed to observe the change of surface potential depending on the hole accumulation. For the KPFM analysis, three different samples were prepared: fresh, control (after 45 h stability test), and NIR (after 45 h stability test) (Supplementary Fig. 34). All the three samples reveal almost identical surface topographies and roughness. The perovskite grains are not clearly visible in the topography from KPFM, as we removed the epoxy after encapsulation. In the SEM data, the surface image of the perovskite device is similar to the topography observed in KPFM; however, it was confirmed that the spiro layer remains preserved as the outermost layer (Supplementary Fig. 35). When compared to the surface work function of fresh sample, both control and NIR samples show an increase of the surface work function value. Especially, the surface potential in the control sample showed a larger increase, rising by 0.7 eV. This substantial increase is attributed to the extensive hole accumulation in HTL during operation. This finding is well matched with XPS analysis, where the C 1s spectra indicates that the HTL is more heavily oxidized due to greater hole accumulation (Supplementary Fig. 36). Therefore, the faster charge transfer reaction of photogenerated electrons reduces the accumulation of holes in the HTL layer. Iodine-related defects have lower activation energy for migration compared to other ions, making them more likely to migrate to charge-accumulated interfaces57–60. This migration leads to phase segregation within the perovskite, which is considered the primary cause of degradation in perovskite devices9,58.

We further performed XRD, cross-sectional SEM, and PL measurements to support the electrochemical characterization. In the XRD spectra of the control device, we observed a reduced peak intensity of the (100) plane and the presence of PbI2 phase with increasing operating time (Supplementary Fig. 37a). Under NIR conditions, the peak intensity of the (100) plane and PbI2 peak ratio were less pronounced than in the control device after 45 h of operation (Supplementary Fig. 37b). The corresponding SEM images of both samples are shown in Supplementary Fig. 37c, d, where pinholes were observed at the spiro-OMeTAD/perovskite interface of the control device after 45 h of operation, consistent with the trap density profiling results.

In steady-state PL analysis, the NIR condition exhibited a negligible PL peak shift during operation, whereas the control device showed a PL peak shift to higher wavelengths after 45 h (Supplementary Fig. 38). This shift is commonly associated with the migration of iodine ions, which often results in phase separation and material degradation, as supported by previous studies61,62 (Supplementary Note 11). To further investigate ion distribution as a function of operating time, we employed time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) (Fig. 3e, f and Supplementary Fig. 39). After 8 h of operation, changes in ion distribution were insignificant; however, a pronounced distribution of I ions towards the HTL was observed after 45 h of operation in both devices. Notably, iodide migration was significantly reduced in the NIR-irradiated device compared to the control, likely due to the enhanced kinetics of the HER, which reduces charge accumulation within the device. Based on the comprehensive analysis of the experimental results, the kinetics of the electrochemical reaction are identified as the principal determinant of stability in perovskite-based water splitting devices.

Effect of NIR irradiation on bubble dynamics

DLCP and ex situ analyses indicate that the performance degradation observed during the initial operation stage of the cathode is not associated with perovskite degradation, suggesting that catalyst stability plays a critical role during this period. To verify this, stability tests were conducted on control and NIR-irradiated Pt-C/CC/FTO electrodes under galvanostatic conditions at 20 mA cm–2 to eliminate the effects of gas production differences between the two conditions (Fig. 4a). The control electrode showed an initial voltage of –0.23 V RHE which rapidly decreased to –0.33 V RHE after 10 h of operation. In contrast, the NIR-irradiated electrode exhibited a much slower voltage decrease from –0.15 V RHE to –0.20 V RHE. Additional stability evaluation through chronoamperometry measurements at –0.25 V RHE (Supplementary Fig. 40) consistently demonstrated enhanced performance stability under NIR irradiation.

To further investigate these results, the structural features of the catalysts were analyzed via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) after 10 h of galvanostatic operation (Fig. 4b–d). Unlike the fresh and NIR-irradiated electrodes, the control electrode exhibited a significant reduction in the quantity of Pt particles. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) confirmed these observations, showing a marked reduction of Pt particles in the control electrode compared to the NIR-irradiated electrode (Supplementary Fig. 41). This finding substantiates that Pt particle detachment during operation is less pronounced under NIR irradiation, confirming the enhanced stability observed during the tests.

The performance degradation of Pt-based catalysts, attributed to agglomeration and detachment due to bubble evolution during operation, was further examined by comparing bubble dynamics between control and NIR-irradiated catalysts63. During potentiostatic tests of the cathode, periodic fluctuations in applied potential and current density were observed (Supplementary Fig. 16), indicative of cycles of nucleation, growth, and departure of gas bubbles on the catalyst surface64. To confirm this, real-time imaging of bubbles on the electrode was conducted (Supplementary Fig. 42). The digital images revealed that bubbles of varying sizes formed across the catalyst, but only a single large bubble significantly influenced photocurrent density fluctuations. This likely occurs because bubble size directly correlates with the deactivation of the active area, leading to a gradual decrease in photocurrent density as the bubble expands65. We opine that bubble size variability arises from the drop-casting method used for electrode fabrication, creating regions that are more favorable for nucleation and bubble coalescence65. To observe the bubble dynamics cycle in greater detail, side-profiling of the Pt-C/CC/FTO electrode under each condition was performed using a high-speed imaging camera (Fig. 4e, f). Notably, NIR irradiation accelerated the successive bubble nucleation, growth, and departure dynamics, shortening the cycle timescale by 21.5% (Fig. 4e, f and Video S2). Despite the faster growth rate, bubbles under NIR irradiation departed at smaller sizes compared to those under the control condition (Fig. 4g, h), likely due to a reduction in the local electrolyte surface tension caused by the photothermally activated catalyst. Reduced surface tension requires less buoyancy force, enabling earlier bubble release66. This was confirmed by finite-element method (FEM) modeling of gas bubbles on a wetted wall, as thermal elevation of electrode rapidly reduces the electrode coverage before departure (Supplementary Fig. 43) (detailed modeling process is described in Methods). This phenomenon also explains the less severe amplitude of current fluctuations observed with NIR irradiation, as the coverage determines the degree of fluctuation (Supplementary Fig. 44, 45). Larger bubbles exhibit greater adhesion, leading to prolonged upward movement on the electrode before decoupling, which imposes shear stress during gas evolution and adversely affects Pt particle adhesion63. Thus, the accelerated bubble dynamics cycle and reduced departure size under NIR irradiation correlate well with the observed reduction in Pt detachment, which is consistent with TEM observations. Moreover, the thermal Marangoni effect, characterized by the formation of temperature gradients, may also contribute to faster bubble departure under NIR conditions and should be considered as a contributing factor67.

The Marangoni convection generated by the thermal gradient in the electrolyte was quantitatively calculated by FEM modeling. Mapping a non-isothermal heat transfer module without the temperature difference between the electrode and electrolyte showed only an infinitesimal velocity change near the bubble due to its oscillation (Fig. 4i). However, with a temperature gradient of 30 K, the electrolyte initiated a circular convection pattern, and the velocity of the electrolyte flow increased nearly four-folds. This micro-stirring effect facilitates the easy departure of bubbles, enabling device operation without the need for external stirring systems that typically require additional input power68. This is relevant to the enhanced operational stability shown in Fig. 1d, which was achieved without the use of an additional stirring system, solely relying on NIR laser irradiation to maintain bubble dynamics and enhanced kinetics.

Degradation mechanism of perovskite-based water splitting system

Figure 5 illustrates the overall degradation mechanism of the perovskite-based water splitting cathode and the direct impact of the photothermal effect on its operational stability. When NIR irradiation is applied to the Pt-C/CC, the local temperature rapidly increases, enhancing the HER kinetics. Also, temperature gradient is formed, inducing thermal Marangoni convection, which accelerates the bubble departure. The rapid gas evolution, characterized by smaller bubble departure sizes, prevents the detachment of Pt particles, thereby improving operational stability. This catalyst degradation mechanism dominates the initial stage of stability decline in the perovskite-based cathode. In addition, the photothermal effect facilitates rapid electron extraction for HER, significantly reducing charge accumulation and iodide migration over extended period of operation, thereby suppressing perovskite degradation. In contrast, without NIR irradiation, sluggish HER kinetics result in accumulation of electrons on the FTO surface and accumulation of holes in the HTL, resulting in increased iodide migration into the HTL. This migration introduces trap states within the HTL, disrupting overall charge transport and accelerating perovskite degradation. These charge transport interruptions worsen with prolonged operation, leading to exacerbated iodide migration and further degradation of the perovskite. Based on these findings, we propose that the degradation of perovskite-based water splitting devices during operation is determined by the stability of the catalyst and the efficiency of charge extraction through electrochemical reactions, both of which are critical factors influencing the overall stability of perovskite-based water splitting systems.

Unassisted water splitting via perovskite-based electrodes

The perovskite-based anode was fabricated by attaching Ni foil to the PSC to prevent electrolyte permeation. To enhance the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalytic activity, a NiFe-layered double hydroxide (NiFeLDH) cocatalyst, hydrothermally synthesized on Ni foam, was attached to the Ni foil (detailed fabrication process is described in Methods and CV values in Supplementary Fig. 51b). The OER performance statistics of the anodes at 1-sun illumination in 0.5 M KPi electrolyte are provided in Supplementary Fig. 46 and Supplementary Table 7. Furthermore, photothermal heating using NIR laser was applied to OER, which improved the performance of anode device (Supplementary Fig. 47). However, stability tests revealed that the NIR irradiated anode exhibited faster degradation and poorer stability compared to the control. Post-measurement characterization further confirmed that prolonged NIR irradiation caused partial oxidation and irreversible damage to the catalyst surface. It should be noted that applying the photothermal effect to OER is not a viable strategy for our system, as it can induce continuous and irreversible damage to the NiFeLDH catalyst.

For unassisted operation without external bias, the cathode and anode were integrated into a parallelly illuminated coplanar system, as illustrated in Fig. 6a. The champion LSV curves of the cathode and anode obtained in 0.5 M KPi were superimposed to determine the operation point of the unbiased device (Fig. 6b). The intersection point of the control cathode and anode was 23.87 mA cm–2 at 0.66 V RHE, while the intersection point of the NIR-irradiated cathode and anode was 24.34 mA cm–2 at 0.76 V RHE. The actual performance of the coplanar device was evaluated using a two-electrode configuration under 1-sun illumination by scanning from –1.2 to 0.2 V (Fig. 6c). Under unbiased conditions (i.e., at 0 V), the control and NIR-irradiated coplanar devices delivered photocurrent densities of 12.08 mA cm–2 and 12.34 mA cm–2, respectively, closely matching the expected operation photocurrent densities which was obtained by halving the photocurrent density intersection point to match the integrated active area. The solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency was calculated using the following equation:

STH(%) = (1.23 V × J mA cm–2) / P0 mW cm–2 × 100% (4)

where J is the photocurrent density at 0 V, and P0 is the power of the incident light. The resulting STH efficiency was 14.89% for the control device and 15.18% for the NIR-irradiated device. Supplementary Fig. 48 and Supplementary Table 8 present the performance of separately prepared 9 coplanar devices, demonstrating reproducible STH efficiency improvements with NIR irradiation. The long-term operational stability of the coplanar device was evaluated using potentiostatic chronoamperometry analysis (Fig. 6d). The control coplanar device barely retained 70% of its initial STH efficiency for 3 h of operation, whereas the NIR-irradiated device maintained 70% of its initial STH efficiency for an extended 115 h. The operational stability statistics for both control and NIR-irradiated coplanar devices are depicted in Supplementary Fig. 49. The H2 production rate of the coplanar device was measured using GC analysis (Fig. 6e). The measured amount of H2 gas was consistent with the theoretical values, confirming high Faradaic efficiencies. Comparative STH efficiency and stability data for previously reported unbiased water-splitting devices are summarized in Supplementary Fig. 50 and Supplementary Table 9. Furthermore, the potential for large-scale applicability of the NIR system is further discussed in Supplementary Note 12.

Discussion

In summary, we present direct operando and in situ observations of charge accumulation in perovskite-based water splitting cathodes and its impact on operational stability utilizing the photothermal effect. This was achieved by integrating a Pt-C/CC catalyst with the cathodes, significantly enhancing the HER kinetics through photothermal activation upon NIR irradiation. The enhanced performance resulted in a ABPE of 20.69%. Moreover, the operational stability of the perovskite-based cathodes was extended from 6 h to 310 h, maintaining ~90% (t90) of its initial photocurrent. Electrochemical analysis under operando conditions effectively monitored suppressed charge accumulation within the multilayer device using identical specimen sets. In situ analyses of the device during operation revealed that reduced charge accumulation led to suppressed iodine migration at the perovskite/HTL interface, with ion migration predominantly occurring during the later stabilized stage of operation. Observations of bubble dynamics showed that NIR irradiation accelerated gas evolution with smaller bubble sizes, effectively preventing detachment of Pt particles and thus enhancing operational stability during the initial stage. Based on these findings, a degradation mechanism for perovskite-based water splitting devices during operation is proposed, providing operando insights into charge accumulation within the perovskite layer, highlighting its role in achieving enhanced operational stability. With improved performance and stability, bias-free solar water splitting achieved a STH efficiency of 15.18%, maintaining 70% of the initial performance for 115 h in a parallelly illuminated coplanar system.

## Methods

Materials

Formamidinium iodide (FAI, > 99.99%), methylammonium bromide (MABr, > 99.99%), and cyclohexylammonium iodide (CHAI, > 99.99%) were sourced from Greatcell Solar (Queanbeyan, Australia). PbI2 (99.99%, trace metals basis) was obtained from TCI Chemicals. Lead bromide (PbBr2 99.999%, trace metals basis), cesium iodide (CsI, 99.999%, trace metals basis), lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (Li-FSI, 98%), dimethylformamide (DMF, anhydrous, 99.8%), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, anhydrous, 99.9%), acetonitrile (anhydrous, 99.8%), chlorobenzene (CB, anhydrous, 99.8%), 2-propanol (IPA, anhydrous, 99.5%), SnCl2·2H2O (99.99%, trace metal basis), 4-tert-butylpyridine (TBP, 96%), tris(2-(1H-pyrazol-1-yl)-4-tert-butylpyridine)cobalt(III) tri[bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide] (KF209 Co TFSI), 2,2′,7,7′-tetrakis(N,N-di-p-methoxyphenylamin-9,9′-spirobifluorene (spiro-OMeTAD), 4-methoxyphenethylamine (98.0%), aquivon, urea (99.0%), thioglycolic acid (TGA, > 99%), methylenediamine dihydrochloride (MDACl2, > 98.0%), potassium iodide (KI, > 99.0%), and Ni foil (100 × 100 mm, thickness 0.1 mm, annealed, 99%), potassium phosphate dibasic (K2HPO4, > 98%), potassium phosphate monobasic (KH2PO4, > 99%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Pt powders with 20% carbon black were obtained from Alfa Aesar (Ward Hill, MA, USA). Carbon cloth was purchased from Wizmac (Korea), and silver paste was obtained from Elcoat (Japan). All chemicals were used as received.

Fabrication of perovskite solar cells

Perovskite solar cells were prepared following previously reported papers69,70. More specifically, an area of 0.5 cm × 2 cm of a 2 cm × 2 cm fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) substrate was etched by thermal scribing method utilizing a laser etching instrument from Korthem Science (Korea). The etched substrates were cleaned with, in the order of, filtered deionized (DI) water, acetone (Duksan, Korea), and ethyl alcohol (Duksan, Korea) for 20 min, respectively. After drying the substrates by a N2 blow gun, the substrates were treated with O2 plasma 10 min. SnO2 was deposited via a chemical bath deposition method. 275 mg of SnCl2·2H2O, 1.25 g of urea, 1.25 mL of HCl (Duksan, Korea), and 25 mL of TGA were dissolved in 100 ml of DI water then was mixed by a magnetic stirring system for 20 minutes. The SnO2 thin film was grown by immersing the FTO substrates in the solution for 2 h at 90 °C. The substrates were washed with IPA and DI water for 10 min, respectively. After drying the substrates, they were annealed at 170 °C for 1 h. The perovskite composition used in this study is (FAPbI3)0.95(MAPbBr3)0.05. 1.4 M FAI, 1.4 M PbI2, 0.023 M MABr, 0.023 M PbBr2, 0.023 M CsI, and 0.5 M MACl with 3.8 mol% MDACl2 were dissolved in a 4:1 mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO for the perovskite ink. After stirring for 15 min, KI was doped (10 μmol) by using a stock solution (166 mg KI in 10 mL DMF). The precursor ink was deposited onto the prepared SnO2/FTO/Glass substrates utilizing a two-step spin-coating process; 12 s at 1000 rpm and then 20 s at 5800 rpm. Ethyl acetate (Duksan, Korea) was used as an antisolvent solution, which 800 µL of the solution was dripped onto the film during the spin-coating process, ~10 s before finishing the second step. The films were annealed using a hot plate for 60 min at 100 °C. The films were cooled to room temperature then a 25 µL of CHAI solution (6 mg CHAI in 1 mL IPA) was spin-coated onto the perovskite surface at 6000 rpm for 30 s, then was annealed at 70 °C for 10 min. The substrate was again cooled to room temperature, then 25 µL of the HTL precursor prepared by 72 mg spiro-OMeTAD dissolved in 1.2 mL chlorobenzene, followed by sequential doping via 17.5 µL Li-TFSI solution (260 mg Li-TFSI in 0.5 mL acetonitrile), 6.85 µL KF209 Co TFSI solution (375 mg KF209 Co TFSI in 1 mL acetonitrile), and 28.8 µL TBP, was spin-coated at 3000 rpm for 30 s. The HTL/perovskite/SnO2/FTO/Glass was aged overnight and then Au electrode of 80-nm was deposited via a thermal evaporator system.

Fabrication of cathode and anode

Cathode and anode were prepared following previously reported papers69,70. More specifically, the cathode was fabricated using a Cu tape with conductive adhesive which was connected to the Au layer and then gently pressed down to form contact. Then, a Cu wire was attached on the Cu tape via silver paste, which was dried in ambient condition for 3 h. Pt-C/CC was prepared by drop casting a Pt-C ink (20 mg of Pt carbon, 0.75 mL of DI water, 0.25 mL of IPA, and 75 µL of Aquivion) onto a carbon cloth and then was dried in room temperature for 24 h. The Pt-C/CC catalyst was applied to the bottom contact (FTO) via silver paste (see Supplementary Fig. 4). The catalyst area for Pt-C/CC/FTO electrode was 0.5 cm2. For the anode, Ni foil was attached to the Au layer with silver paste, and NiFeLDH/Ni foam was fabricated by dissolving Ni(NO3)2·6H2O (0.3 g), Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (0.38 g), and urea (0.6 g) in 70 mL of DI water under sonication for 15 min. The precursor solution and Ni foam were then subjected to hydrothermal synthesis in a Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave, followed by annealing of the resulting Ni foam for 12 h at 120 °C. The Ni foams were washed with DI water and acetone for 5 min each and dried for 24 h at 80 °C. The mass loading was ~1.5 mg cm–2 and was calculated by weighing the Ni foam before and after hydrothermal synthesis. The NiFeLDH/Ni foam catalyst was attached to Ni foil using silver paste and sealed with epoxy resin, and a Cu wire was attached to the FTO side using silver paste. The catalyst area of both Pt-C/CC/FTO and NiFeLDH/Ni foam ranged from 0.06 to 0.1 cm2.

Film characterizations

The phase evolution of the perovskite film was characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Miniflex 600 instrument, Woodlands, TX, USA). The surface morphology of the annealed samples was examined via field emission SEM (JSM-7800F, JEOL Ltd., Japan) and contact-mode atomic force microscopy (AFM, NX-10 AFM, Park Systems, Korea). ToF-SIMS measurements (TOF-SIMS V, ION-TOF GmbH, Germany) were performed using pulsed primary ions from a Cs+ (1 keV, 56.8 nA) liquid-metal ion gun for sputtering, and Bi+ and Bi3+ pulsed primary ion beams for analysis (30 keV). Raman spectra of the catalyst were obtained with a confocal Raman microscope (WITec, Germany) with an excitation wavelength of 532 nm. TEM (JEM-ARM200F, JEOL, Japan) analysis was performed at 200 kV to investigate the detachment of Pt particles. The profiling distance (X) from the junction barrier is given by: X = εε0A / C.

PV measurements

Similar setup in a previous report was utilized19. Specifically, a solar simulator (Sol3A Class AAA, Oriel Instruments, Stratford, CT, USA) was set to 1.5 AM and 1-sun conditions (100 mW cm–2) to test the performance of PSCs. The setup was calibrated using a Si reference cell (Newport Corporation, Irvine, USA). The active area of the PSC set to 0.06 cm2 using a photomask. Voltage was swept from –0.1 to 1.5 V with a rate of 0.50 V s–1 with a dwell time of 50 ms at each point to obtain J-V curves. A quantum efficiency measurement system (QEX10, PV Measurements, Inc.) was utilized to extract external quantum efficiency (EQE) spectra. J-V measurements and EQE spectra were obtained under ambient conditions (RH 15–20%, 23–25 °C).

Voltammetry analyses

A three-electrode system with a Pt wire counter electrode and an Ag/AgCl/KCl (4M) reference electrode in 0.5 M KPi (pH 7) was employed under simulated solar illumination (AM 1.5G; Newport Corporation, USA). 0.5 M KPi (pH 7±0.2) was prepared by dissolving K2HPO4 (9.343 g) and KH2PO4 (6.309 g) in 200 ml of DI water and was stored at room temperature (23–25 °C) for short-term (<1 week) use. The ohmic resistance of the 0.5 M KPi is 14.5±1.4 Ω and was calculated by EIS results with the catalytic area of 0.1 cm2. Pt wire of 1 mm in diameter with a length of 20 cm was used as the counter electrode. The reference electrode was prepared and calibrated before use by measuring the potential difference against a new Ag/AgCl/KCl (4M). LSV measurements were conducted with a reverse sweep to ensure reliability and have not been iR corrected. All measurements were controlled using a potentiostat (SI1287, Solartron, UK), and the applied potentials were adjusted to the RHE scale for comparison with previously reported values: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.059 pH + 0.197. The ABPE was calculated using the LSV curve according to the following equations:

ABPE(%) = (JHER × V) / P0 × 100% (5)

ABPE(%) = (JOER × (1.23 – V)) / P0 × 100% (6)

where JHER and JOER are the measured photocurrent densities, V is the applied bias, and P0 is the incident illumination power density (i.e., AM 1.5G, 100 mW cm–2). Voltammetry analyses were conducted using a NIR laser (MDL-H-808 3W 808 nm infrared diode laser, CNI laser, China). The exposed area of the perovskite-based electrodes ranged from 0.06 to 0.1 cm2, matching the catalytic active area. ECSA measurements were conducted by calculating the average current density from the anodic (ja) and cathodic (jc) current density from corresponding CV curves, Δj = (ja – jc) / 2. Each set of CV curves was parted by a 3 min OCV to avoid any unnecessary charge buildup. Electrode area was 0.6 cm2 and specific capacitance 0.02 mF cm–2. EIS was performed using a potentiostat with a frequency analyzer (1260, Solartron, UK). Polarization and series resistances of the cathodes were measured at potentials ranging from 1.0 to 0.8 V RHE across a frequency range of 0.1 Hz to 300 kHz under 1-sun illumination with a 10-mV alternating-current amplitude. Mott-Schottky, DLCP, and C-V analyses were conducted at a fixed frequency of 10 kHz using the same frequency analyzer. The C-V analysis provided the carrier densities at the edge of the depletion region:

Nc(X) = 2 / (qεε0A2 d(1/C2) / dV) (7)

The profiling distance (X) from the junction barrier is given by: X = εε0A / C.

For the DLCP measurement, the voltage (V) was scanned from 0 V to the open circuit voltage (i.e. 1.1 V) for the hybrid device. The DLCP method employs a series of variable δV (20–200 mV) to measure the junction capacitance and extract capacitance contributions from trap states by analyzing higher-order terms. The capacitance at each δV was recorded and fitted with a polynomial function: C = C0 + C1δV + C2(δV)2 + … to determine C0 and C1. Using C0 and C1, the total carrier density (N), including both free carriers and trap density at a profiling distance X from the junction barrier, is calculated by:

Nc(X) = C03 / (2qεε0A2C1) (8)

The profiling distance (X) from the junction barrier is given by: X = εε0A / C0.

IPCE, IMVS, IMPS, and TPC measurements were conducted using an electrochemical workstation (Zennium, Zahner, Germany) and a potentiostat (PP211, Zahner, Germany). Data fitting was performed using ZView software. Gas chromatography (6500 GC system, YL Instrument, Anyang, Korea) with a pulsed discharge detector and a molecular sieve column was used to confirm H2 evolution. Rubber bulkheads were employed to seal all connections of the device, preventing gas leakage from the quartz.

High-speed imaging

High-speed imaging and time lapse of bubble formation, growth, and departure on catalyst were conducted using a high-speed camera (C320, Vision Research, New Jersey, USA) and a digital single-lens reflex (DSLR) camera (D5300, Nikon, Tokyo, Japan), respectively. Both the high-speed camera and DSLR camera were equipped with a 2X tele-converter (TELEPLUS MC7 AF 2x DGX, Kenko, Tokyo, Japan) and a 105-mm F2.8 macro lens (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan).

COMSOL Multiphysics modeling

Bubble departure in an electrolyte under varying electrode temperatures (0–30 K) was modeled using COMSOL Multiphysics (COMSOL, Stockholm, Sweden), with temperature information from experimental data. The geometry consisted of a water domain (15 mm × 15 mm) and a bubble (radius 1–2 mm) positioned at the center of the wetted wall (electrode). The laminar flow module incorporated gravity to simulate natural convection. A level set module defined two fluids: air (bubble) and water (surrounding medium), with no-flow boundaries at the top and bottom. Heat transfer was modeled using a temperature gradient defined as T = Tamb + ΔT × (x – xlim)/xlim, where Tamb = 293.15 K, ΔT = 0–30 K, and xlim = 1 mm. A wetted wall condition was applied with a slip length proportional to the minimum element size and a contact angle of π/3. Non-isothermal flow accounted for the effects of temperature on fluid behavior and bubble departure.

Data availability

All data generated in this study are provided in the Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

### Reviewer 1

In this paper, the authors investigate the role of charge accumulation on operational stability through operando catalytic modulation via near-infrared (NIR) toggling on a photothermal catalyst. The NIR irradiation enhances HER kinetics and inhibits charge accumulation and ion migration in the perovskite layer. As a result, a record-high STH efficiency and enhanced operational stability were obtained. The work is interesting and presents advances in the field. I recommend it for publication after dealing with the concerns listed below.
1. For the stability test in Figure.1d, a sudden photocurrent drop from ~20 mA/cm2 to 0 was observed after ~310 h tracking. Similar results can be seen in Figure. 6d. The authors need to explain the reasons beneath.
2. On page 8 line 180, how do the authors define the Jph fluctuation period? How are the Jph fluctuation period results obtained from Sup. Fig. 16?
3. On page 9 line 203, the authors showed an increased ECSA value under NIR irradiation. Were the results obtained from the same device? I suggest the author monitor ECSA change on the same device during the continuous process from NIR irradiation off to on and then to off.
4. On page 11 line 252, the authors perform TPC analysis to observe charge accumulation. Please give more test method details (e.g., bias conditions) in the Method section and give a specific explanation of how the charge flows to generate the reverse current.
5. On page 15 line 368, stability tests under galvanostatic conditions were performed. Since charge carrier and ion distribution are related to bias conditions, will the different voltages influence the stability?
6. Mott-Schottky analysis: The device capacity is quite different between Figure. S24 and S29 for the control and target devices, is it because the slight differences in device architecture?
7. If the solar simulator light intensity is decreased to reduce photogenerated charge carrier density, or the catalyst and the electrolyte are changed to enhance the HER catalytic activity, will the charge carrier accumulation and ion migration be inhibited?
8. On page 19 line 454, the authors built up an unassisted water-splitting system. Will NIR irradiation have similar effects on the OER side?

### Reviewer 2

This paper looks at the effect of NIR irradiation on a catalyst modified cathode attached to a perovskite solar cell. I cannot recommend the paper for publication at the moment as I have many questions about the reliability and accuracy of the techniques used as well as questions about whether the results have been interpreted correctly.
(1) The authors discuss that this is an encapsulated solar cell which is connected in series with a catalyst coated electrode. There is some discussion of the configuration and why it was chosen, but I think there needs to be clearer explanation for why it is better to submerge the solar cell, rather than keeping it outside the solution and connecting the photoelectrode with a slightly longer wire?
(2) Does the NIR heating of the carbon electrode create a temperature gradient and thereby cause a large increase in convective stirring? Is there an increase in performance due to increased mass transfer of e.g. the reactants and products to and from the electrode? Is it possible to differentiate whether the improvements are due to enhanced kinetics, or rather enhanced mass transport? There are papers that suggest that the HER on Pt nanoparticles is mass transport limited, increased mass transport would therefore legitimately increase current (e.g. https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsenergylett.1c00246). As far as I can see this has not been investigated? The bubble evidence supports this?
(3) It is stated that NIR irradiation significantly enhanced both the photocurrent and the photovoltage. I can understand how the photocurrent is affected, but can the authors better explain why the photovoltage (by which I mean the open circuit photovoltage) is different? In this case the cell is at open circuit and no charge is being extracted through the contacts, how can heating of the contact influence the open circuit photovoltage inside the device?
(4) The increased catalytic activity is partly attributed to an increased surface area which is taken from measurements of the double layer capacitance. A larger surface area is measured under NIR. I would like to see this measured several times (e.g. control, NIR, control, NIR, control) to rule out other mechanisms such as irreversible roughening of the electrode?
(5) Impedance spectroscopy shows that the low frequency arc of the control device has a larger diameter (attributed to higher Rct) at the same voltage versus RHE. Given the complexity of the impedance spectroscopy of perovskites, can the authors give evidence that the low frequency arc is measuring RCT and not some kind of ion modulated current? Would the diameter of the arc not be expected to be quite different as at the same applied voltage versus RHE the two systems are in different states? E.g. at 0.9 V versus RHE the control cell is effectively at open circuit whereas the NIR cell still has a photocurrent of over 20 mA and may not have a linear response.
(6) Mott-Schottky analysis is used to determine that there is no change in band-bending in the bulk perovskite. Mott-Schottky very rarely measured band bending in perovskite cells (there are many papers showing just how problematic it is as a technique for perovskites and proving that it rarely measures the space charge layer) and a great deal of work is needed here for the authors to convince us that they are actually measuring band bending. I suspect that none of the Mott-Schottky analysis here is valid?
(7) IMVS is measured – but the interpretation is far from clear. It should mirror the EIS results at open circuit.
(8) IMPS is measured and the data is fitted to extract ktrans and krec. All the EIS and IMPS plots need to be plotted isotropically. IMPS of perovskite solar cells measured at high frequencies measures the RC time constant of the devices (RseriesCgeo). Are the authors able to show that this is not what is being measured here? The data for both cells looks very similar, especially when it is claimed that the NIR strongly changes the kinetics. It is straightforward to calculate the RC time constant and to compare it with 1/RC from the semi-circle maximum? This needs to be ruled out.
(9) Can the authors show that DLCP and CV methods actually measure the carrier trap density in their devices? Typically, these techniques do not accurately measure traps in perovskite devices as the ion migration dominates the response. All the same issues as for Mott Schottky analysis apply, there are many papers on this which are not discussed.

### Reviewer 3

The present manuscript discusses degradation of perovskite-based photocathode caused by charge accumulation. Comparison with and without NIR irradiation on HER catalyst and various characterization during the degradation found that sluggish HER kinetics led to the charge accumulations in the semiconductor and its degradation. The present manuscript would provide design guidelines for durable photocathodes which can be potentially considered in various semiconductors. However, my concern is what would be the original cause of the degradation. Is it due to either the catalysts degradation caused by bubbles or poor HER kinetics in the absence of NIR? Additional simple control measurements would further clarify their claims before its publication in Nat. Commun. Please find the following questions.
Fig. 1c
The authors claim that “the photothermal effect induced by NIR irradiation increased the catalyst’s temperature, thereby accelerating HER kinetics and enhancing both Jph and Von.” Why Von changes by HER kinetics? Von should be at 0 mA/cm2 where HER kinetics does not involve. Does the Von shift come from the thermodynamics of HER? The authors may be able to discuss the shift from Nernst equations. It may also help to evaluate the local temperature on the catalyst not just by IR camera.
Fig. S19
Tafel slope on Pt-C/CC/FTO was found to be reduced by NIR. If we simply follow Tafel equation or Butler-Volmer equation, the slope should increase at the elevated temperature. The authors can discuss the observed change in detail. I may consider that the improved kinetics helps to suppress the coverage of H leading to the smaller Tafel slope. See Sci. Rep. 5 (2015) 13801.
Additionally, can they show LSV of Pt-C/CC/FTO after the stability tests? It helps readers to observe how the overpotential increased after Pt detachment.
Local heating
Local heating by NIR seems to play an important role. It is also known that kinetic loss on electrocatalysts causes a local heating. Can they compare NIR power density and local heating from HER catalysis? The authors can evaluate the local heating (W/cm2) due to HER from the operating current density (A/cm2) and overpotential (V). Overpotential can be roughly evaluated from LSV at their operating current density. This analysis helps the readers to get an idea on the power density levels needed to heat up.
The huge bubbles and their detachments were claimed to be the cause of Pt detachment and degradation of HER. The authors limited systems without additional stirring. Can they perform control measurements with stirring and without NIR. For example, stability test of Pt-C/CC/FTO (like Fig4a), stability of photocathode (like Fig. 1d), and bubble observation (like Fig4e). This comparison will help to clarify the major cause on the degradation of photocathode either from bubbles or HER kinetics. If the bubbles are removed efficiently without NIR irradiation and HER activity is maintained at room temperature, does the photocathode degrade? Or, is the improvement of HER kinetics (like Fig. S19a) necessary?
If the Pt-C degraded by the bubbles in the absence of NIR is used for the fresh perovskite, can it still maintain the stability with NIR irradiation?
Kinetics of charge consumptions should be an important factor determining the degradation of perovskite. Simple measurements using PV setup (without the electrolytes and electrocatalysts) can be performed with solar irradiation at OCV and short circuit conditions while measuring IV response at certain periods. Keeping at OCV (0 mA cm2) under solar irradiation leads to charge accumulation which would cause degradation of semiconductor while keeping at the short circuit is the case of extremely fast kinetics case minimizing the charge accumulations. I believe the degradation observed in the photocathode would be positioned between them.
Implementation potential of NIR local heating technique
Because the authors also emphasize its record high efficiency and large-scale applications, it would be nice to discuss how the natural solar irradiation would be managed to implement this technique in a real device. Do we need to separate NIR from the natural solar using some mirror? In their study, NIR was obtained from laser with various power. When we irradiate a unit area of perovskite, can we obtain sufficient NIR power after the split of natural sunlight? The authors can discuss its potential based on the standard solar spectrum.
Supplementary Note 9
The onset potential of 1:1_control in Supplementary Note Fig 7b is quite high compared with those on other large scale samples and small devices in Main text. What is the reason? Does the cathodic photocurrent come from HER or reduction of large area catalysts region which may be reduced more easily?
